So the ketogenic diet, unbeknownst to most people, was actually developed a hundred years ago, 1921, by a physician for one and only one purpose-- to treat epilepsy. It wasn't developed as a weight loss diet. It wasn't developed as the diet that all human beings should follow. And the reason it was developed is because of this longstanding observation, since the time of Hippocrates, that fasting can stop seizures. Now, fasting is not a healthy diet. Fasting is the process of no diet. So we now understand a tremendous amount of science. Most people think going without food is bad. And they equate it with starvation. But in fact, when we go without food, it causes tremendous shifts in metabolism-- both brain and body metabolism. And it puts the body into a mode of autophagy, and conservation of resources, and all sorts of things that are beneficial to human health. And this is why fasting has been used as a therapeutic intervention in almost every culture, in almost every religion for a millennia. But for the most part, that was all thought to be religious folklore. That was just crazy talk. And those stupid people way back then thought God cured everything. And so they fasted.   16. @葉瓊鞠: Concept: Ketogenic Diet Makes Mitochondria Less Efficient
Definition of “Less Efficient” Mitochondria

Normally, mitochondria generate ATP (energy) by oxidizing nutrients (mainly glucose).

Efficiency = how much ATP is made per oxygen molecule used.

On a ketogenic diet, mitochondria may:

Use more oxygen per unit of ATP (i.e., lower P/O ratio).

Generate more heat instead of storing energy as ATP.

Engage in mild mitochondrial uncoupling (increased proton leak).

Why This Happens:

Ketones (e.g., β-hydroxybutyrate) enter different metabolic pathways than glucose.

Leads to:

Greater NADH/FADH2 input, altering electron transport chain (ETC) dynamics.

More reactive oxygen species (ROS), which triggers mild uncoupling as protection.

Activation of UCPs (Uncoupling Proteins) like UCP2/3.

🔥 Effect on Fat Loss
Counterintuitive Insight:

Although “less efficient” mitochondria make less ATP, the body burns more fuel (fat/ketones) to meet energy demands.

This “wasteful” process increases calorie expenditure.

Net Effect:

✅ Increased Fat Oxidation: Because more fat must be burned to produce the same energy.

✅ Higher Thermogenesis: More heat is produced, increasing total energy expenditure.

✅ Supports Weight Loss: Despite lower mitochondrial efficiency, total fat loss may improve.

Simplified Analogy:
Think of a car engine that burns more gasoline to go the same distance — it’s inefficient, but uses more fuel overall.

- Does Keto Really Improve Mitochondrial Biogenesis? - Functional and Integrative Wellness Guru: Kind: captions Language: en Does keto really improve mitochondrial biogenesis? Imagine your cells as tiny power plants, constantly working to keep you energized. Now, what if a certain diet could help these power plants grow stronger and more efficient? That's what we're exploring today. The ketogenic diet, which is high in fats and very low in carbohydrates, has been linked to boosting the creation of new mitochondria inside your cells. Mitochondria are the structures responsible for producing energy from the food you eat. When you follow a ketogenic diet, your body produces more ketone bodies, especially beta hydroxybutyrate. These ketones do more than just supply energy. They act as signals to your cells. These signals activate important regulators like PGC-1 alpha cert 3 and UCP2. These molecules work together to promote the growth of new mitochondria and improve their efficiency. Studies in animals and cells show that ketogenic diets increase mitochondrial markers, boost oxygen use, and raise the NAD plus to NADH ratio, which indicates better mitochondrial function. In mice with mitochondrial problems, a ketogenic diet can stimulate the production of more mitochondria, helping cells generate energy better despite existing issues. Human studies also support this idea. When people on a ketogenic diet exercise, their muscle cells show increased mitochondrial capacity. This means their cells can burn fat more efficiently and produce energy with less oxygen, which is a sign of healthier mitochondria. From a wellness point of view, this suggests that ketogenic diets can help improve cellular energy production. This is especially useful for aging, metabolic problems, or mitochondrial diseases. The diet may also reduce oxidative stress and inflammation which can damage mitochondria over time. You might consider using a ketogenic approach to support mitochondrial health if you are dealing with age- related muscle loss, metabolic syndrome, or neurodeenerative conditions. However, it's important to remember that not everyone will see the same benefits. Athletes with already high mitochondrial function might not experience much change. In short, ketogenic diets do seem to promote the growth and function of mitochondria through specific molecular pathways. This makes them a promising dietary strategy for boosting cellular energy and supporting overall metabolic health.

CoQ10 ultimately gets converted to ubiquinol, and it's ubiquinol which the body needs and uses.
1) if you have a CoQ10 genetic SNP (a change in your genes), then you may not be able to convert enough or any CoQ10 (ubiquinone) to its usable form of ubiquinol. 
2) also: if you are deficient in magnesium, you may not be able to convert CoQ10 to ubiquinol.
3) so even if you test as having adequate CoQ10 levels, this may not give you the correct info to assess your health. Why? Because if you can't convert it to the active form (ubiquinol), then your body will be deficient. Should you test for ubiquinol? I've learned it's a rather 'flaky' particle, and breaks down rather quickly after a blood draw, making it difficult to measure. So if someone has a CoQ10 genetic SNP, they may just want to supplement with ubiquinol; unfortunately, it is more expensive.

And they're an incredibly clean, efficient fuel source, powerful enough to run the most energy hungry organs you have, like your brain and your heart. So, how does this whole fuel switch actually happen? Well, for a few hours after a meal, it's simple. You're running on glucose. But after about 12 hours of fasting, your liver starts to dip into its glycogen reserves. By the 24-hour mark, those reserves are pretty much gone, and that's when the liver seriously ramps up ketone production. It's your body adapting in real time, making sure your brain especially has a constant supply of highquality energy. But here's the thing, being fuel, that's only half the story. And this is where it gets really, really cool. It turns out one ketone in particular is the real star of the show. It's time to meet a powerful messenger molecule called BHB. That's beta hydroxybutyrate or just BHB for short. And this is where the science just gets fascinating because what researchers are finding is that BHB is so much more than just a unit of energy. It's also a powerful signaling molecule. So BHB basically has two jobs. The first is fuel, which we've talked about. It travels to your tissues, gets converted, and boom, energy. But its second job, wow, this is the game changer. BHB also travels right into the nucleus of your cells, the command center, and it starts to change how your actual DNA is read. I mean, think about that. It's not just powering the house. It's rewriting the daily instructions for how to run the place. And that idea, a molecule from our own body rewriting our to-do list, brings us right to our next section. How BHB is literally talking to your genes. Okay, to really get this, we need to touch on a concept called epigenetics. Now, that sounds super complex, I know, but the idea is actually pretty simple. It's just the process of changing which of your genes are turned on or off without actually changing the DNA code itself. It's all about gene expression. Here's a fantastic way to picture it. Imagine your DNA is this massive ancient cookbook with thousands and thousands of recipes. Those are your genes. Now, epigenetics doesn't rewrite any of the recipes themselves. Instead, it's like the chef who decides which recipes to cook today. And BHB, it acts like a little molecular bookmark telling the chef, "Hey, read this one. This is a really good protective recipe we should be using right now." So, what kind of recipes is BHP bookmarking? Well, the research shows it acts as something called an HDAC inhibitor. Now, that's a mouthful, I know, but what it basically means is it makes all these good protective genes easier for the cell to read and use. And by doing that one thing, it helps boost our antioxidant defenses. It tamps down inflammation and it improves our overall metabolism. It's basically telling ourselves to activate their best defense and repair programs. You know, that anti-inflammatory effect is so mind-blowing that it really deserves its own moment. So, let's dive into how BHB is quite literally putting out the fire of chronic inflammation. Okay, another simple analogy for a really complex system here. Inside our cells, we have this ultra sensitive smoke detector. It's called the NLRP3 inflammosome. Its job is crucial, right? It sounds the alarm against real threats. But here's the problem. In many chronic diseases, that alarm gets stuck in the on position, just blaring away and causing this constant, damaging, lowgrade inflammation. And you do not have to take my word for it. Just look at this. This is the visual proof straight from the research paper. In the image on the left without BHB, you see all those bright green specks? That's the alarm system going nuts. It's a crystal clear picture of inflammation in action. But now look at the image on the right. When the scientists simply added BHB, poof, the specs are pretty much gone. The alarm has been silenced. So, how on earth does it do this? Well, it's actually incredibly elegant. BHB basically stops the alarm from ever being assembled by regulating potassium inside the cell. It prevents the different pieces of that inflammosome from clicking together. It's not just disarming the alarm, it's preventing it from ever being built in the first place. So all of this incredible science, it all builds up to this one massive question. Could this natural molecule, something our own bodies make, represent a whole new class of medicine? And here's why that question is so urgent. That faulty alarm, that overactive NLRP3 inflammosome is implicated in a terrifying list of modern chronic diseases. We're talking type 2 diabetes. We're talking atherosclerosis, that's the hardening of the arteries, Alzheimer's disease, gout, and even some aspects of age related decline. So, finding a way to calm this system down is a really, really big deal. And this isn't just speculation. The researchers themselves in one of the world's top medical journals concluded with this powerful statement, and I'll quote it directly. dietary or pharmacological approaches to elevate BHB holds promise in reducing the severity of multiple NLRP3 mediated chronic inflammatory diseases. I mean the potential here is just absolutely enormous. And so that leaves us with this final provocative thought. Could a molecule our body already makes one that we can increase naturally just through diet or fasting, could that actually be the key to fighting some of our most devastating chronic diseases? The science seems to be suggesting that's a question we can no longer afford to ignore.

For brief background though, Dom, can you give us a description or explanation of how an injury to the brain can result in neuromabolic crisis? >> Yeah, sure. Traumatic brain injury is a growing concern, even a crisis, especially in older adults. And traumatic brain injury initiates a neuromabolic crisis and you have an an impact the the injury itself and then that that quickly causes a neuromabolic crisis. The first actually a few hours you get a hypoglycolytic effect and then you get this protracted glucose hypom metabolism in the brain that is a hallmark characteristic of chronic traumatic encphylopathy for example and that glucose hypom metabolism leads to things like post-traumatic epilepsy depression and psychiatric disorders. So you have the impact and the energetic crisis which is the driver for the neuroinflammation and not the opposite way around and now new evidence now this is becoming more accepted. So you have the energy crisis, impaired, you know, energy from blood flow for one thing, low levels of oxygenation and just impaired glucose metabolism. one important way in which this is achieved is by increasing oxidative capacity which is the ability of your muscle cells to consume oxygen now oxidative capacity not only depends on the availability of oxygen which is what most people tend to focus on but it also critically relies on your mitochondria which are the tiny units inside of your muscle cells that are actually consuming oxygen to produce ATP which is the energetic currency of the cell and this is really important you want your ATP production to exceed your ATP consumption in order to enhance or maximize your performance and avoid muscle fatigue at the level of the mitochondria there are two ways in which you can increase your oxidative capacity one is by increasing the total number of mitochondria and two is by increasing the efficiency of your already existing mitochondria Studies have shown that just one session of high-intensity interval training results in the production of new mitochondria thereby increasing the total number of mitochondri mria per muscle cell but in order to make new mitochondria this requires your existing mitochondria to copy their genome and this is done by enzymes that require magnesium as a co-actor the magnesium ion sits inside of the enzyme and activates it so that it can do its job what this means is that if your magnesium levels are low then you're going to have a difficult time making new mitochondria during exercise therefore compromising your performance the second way you can maximize your mitochondria is by making your existing mitochondria more efficient at producing ATP it is well known that during exercise oxidative stress damages your mitochondria and dampens their ability to produce ATP but your mitochondria have the ability to repair this damage using the same magnesium dependent enzymes that I just mentioned the bottom line is you want to make sure your magnesium levels are within the adequate range in order to maximize your mitochondria by a the ability to produce new mitochondria and B making your existing mitochondria more efficient at repairing damage so in conclusion I highly recommend you get your magnesium levels tested and when in doubt increase your consumption of dark green leafy vegetables such as spinach and kale or almonds which are all high in magnesium I'm Dr Rhonda Patrick and I'll catch you next   4. @DA-uz8qb [1 likes]: Dom's insight, around 7:30, is poignant. It takes a while to transition from a non-ketogenic, high-carbohydrate diet to ketogenic diets, as the enzymes and other protein structures involved in efficient ketone processing 'catch up' to the global switch in primary fuel source. 

I have heard from multiple sources that it can take many months to be "keto adapted", and that is assuming strict adherence to a ketogenic diet during those months. I imagine this transition will be easier, in general, if diet was not extremely metabolically damaging for years on-end (see: high veg oil, high carb, high sugar), but nonetheless, it WILL take time. 

The point is: in the transition process, on a high fat diet, your blood will be replete with ketone bodies floating around, so much so that there will be an excess of ketone supply vs. ketone demand/metabolic processing ability. Your machinery has not caught up yet. Ketones like acetone and b-OHB will be shed through the breath (acetone) and in the urine (b-OHB). All this to say, a measurably high ketone level may reflect an INEFFICIENCY in ketone metabolism, rather than something that is inherently better than a lower level of ketones in the blood (as is seen in later, "keto adapted" state).

So perhaps the take-home point, which he makes a couple seconds later, is that in sustained ketogenic nutrition, INSULIN remains low, excess glucose is allowed to be metabolized and discarded, and the preferred, abundant and healthier fuel is now metabolized ad libitum. And the more you can stay in a state where primary and majority of metabolic need is met with fatty acids and ketones, the better.

- 132: The Hidden Power of Ketones: Fueling + Signaling with Dr. Ben Bikman: Kind: captions Language: en Ketones aren't just fuel. They act like hormones. For decades, ketones were dismissed as metabolic leftovers, then downgraded to backup energy when glucose runs low. But one ketone, beta hydroxybutyrate, does far more than just make ATP. It actually sends signals. BHB can bind to receptors, reduce inflammation, protect mitochondria, and even change how genes are expressed. That's extremely rare in biology. Most nutrients provide calories. Most hormones send messages. Ketones do both. When ketones rise during fasting, exercise, or a ketogenic diet, cells receive a coordinated message. Reduce inflammation, increase resilience, and protect energy production. Ketones aren't just an alternative fuel. They are a metabolic signal. This is lecture 132 of the metabolic classroom. Looking to improve your own metabolic health? Visit insuliniq.com for courses, coaching, consultations, and a 10-day free community membership trial. Welcome to the Metabolic Classroom. I'm Ben Bickman, metabolic scientist and professor of cell biology. In today's mini lecture, we are exploring one of the most fascinating developments in metabolic research over the past several decades. The discovery that ketones, specifically beta hydroxybutyrate or BHB. They're not just fuel molecules, but potent signaling agents. For decades, biochemistry textbooks treated ketones as metabolic garbage. Then they were finally upgraded to a backup fuel, a sort of metabolic plan B that kicks in if glucose runs low. But we now understand that this view was far too limited. BHB does something genuinely remarkable in the world of biology. It functions simultaneously as both a calorie providing nutrient and a signaling molecule that can alter gene expression, reduce inflammation, and protect our mitochondria. This dual identity is actually quite rare in biology. Think about it. Most signaling molecules, hormones, neurotransmitters or cytoines don't provide calories or any any energy at all. And most nutrients like glucose, fats, etc., which can provide energy, are not considered signaling molecules in any classic sense. But BHB blurs these boundaries completely. It's like discovering that gasoline doesn't just power your car's engine, but it also unlocks the doors. So, today we're going to unpack this signaling story. We'll talk about specific receptors. We'll discuss how and which tissues respond to these signals, and we'll explore what this means for inflammation and mitochondrial function. First, let's establish a foundation. Beta hydroxybutyrate or BHB is the most abundant of the three ketone bodies as they're classically called and BHB makes up roughly 70% of all of the circulating ketones in the body. The other two are accetoacetate and acetone. BHB is primarily synthesized in liver mitochondria when fatty acids are being oxidized at a high rate. Here's an important structural detail that will matter later. BHB is a chyal molecule, meaning it exists in two mirror image forms. The body mostly produces what's called DBHB, but it's also sometimes indicated as RBHB. This is the majority form that we make. The L form or sometimes known as S form is also made and it can be about 10% of what we have circulating in our blood when we are making our own ketones. And that LBH, as you'll see, can both be consumed as energy, but for the context of this lecture, also act as a signaling molecule. Now, unfortunately, we're just really starting to learn about LBH with though ketones were long considered a metabolic garbage, even once they were considered not to be garbage, LBHB was sometimes still considered garbage. For those who need a quick refresher on epigenetics, histones are proteins around which DNA is wrapped. By upregulating antioxidant gene expression, BHB essentially preconditions cells to handle oxidative stress. But even further, the cell becomes much better equipped to neutralize those radicals before they cause damage. There's another layer to this epigenetic story. This is a newly discovered post translational modification where the BH where the beta hydroxybuterral group is coalently attached to lysine residues on histones and other proteins. This represents just another one more way that BHB can directly couple metabolic state to gene expression. Not just by inhibiting enzymes that erase acetilation marks, but by providing a substrate for an entirely distinct type of histone modification. Let me review what we've covered and focus on the mitochondrial implications because I think this is where the signaling story of BHB becomes most relevant to metabolic health. First, BHB as a fuel. When peripheral tissues oxidize BHB, the conversion back to accetoacetate generates NADH. The subsequent entry of acetal COA into the citrate cycle generates additional NADH and another reducing equivalent, FADH2. These reducing equivalents feed the electron transport system to produce a lot of ATP. Some researchers have suggested that ketone metabolism may be thermodynamically more efficient than glucose metabolism that the PTO ratio or the ATP that is generated per oxygen consumed may be slightly higher. The evidence for this is debated but what's clear is that ketones are an extremely efficient fuel that can sustain tissues even when glucose is limited and indeed do so very well. Second, oxidative stress mitigation through HDAC inhibition and the resulting upregulation of FOX 03A and other antioxidant genes. BHB helps cells cope with the reactive oxygen species that are an inevitable byproduct of mitochondrial respiration. This is particularly important in high energy demand tissues like the brain and the heart where mitochondrial density is high and oxidative damage can be devastating. Third, inflammation and mitochondrial health are intimately connected. Chronic inflammation damages mitochondria. Pro-inflammatory cytoines like interlucan 1 beta can impair mitochondrial function, reduce ATP production, and increase reactive oxygen species generation in a vicious cycle. By inhibiting the NLRP3 inflammosome and reducing interlucan 1 beta production, BHB protects mitochondria from this inflammation induced damage. Fourth, the GPR 109A pathway on immune cells appears to shift them toward phenotypes that are less damaging to host tissues. The neuroprotective macrofasages we discussed earlier likely represent cells that clean up damage without perpetuating inflammation. Exactly what you want when tissues are under any kind of stress. And fifth, consider that all of these effects happen simultaneously. When you fast, when you follow a ketogenic diet or you are consuming exogenous ketones in the form of go BHB, your BHB levels rise and you get this coordinated multipathway response, reduced inflammation through NLRP3 inhibition, enhanced oxi antioxidant defenses through HDAC inhibition, and modulation of immune cell behavior through GPR 109A. This is not one drug hitting one target. It's a fundamental metabolic signal that orchestrates cellular resilience. Before I conclude, let me briefly touch on where this science is heading. Understanding BHB as a signaling molecule has opened up new therapeutic possibilities that go beyond simply recommending d fasting or ketogenic diets. Exogenous ketone supplements, specifically go BHB in the form of the ketone salts or the ketone or the BHB acid, can elevate blood BHB levels without requiring dietary carbohydrate restriction. Clinical trials are now are now examining whether these supplements can provide anti-inflammatory and neuroprotective effects in various conditions. For conditions like Alzheimer's disease, where patients have lower BHB levels and impaired brain glucose metabolism, ketone supplementation offers a way to both provide an alternative fuel and engage these protective signaling pathways. There's similar benefits in the heart. In the heart failure research space, there's growing interest in ketones as a superfuel for the failing heart, which often has impaired glucose and fatty acid metabolism. ## 🎙 節目概要
在 *《Boost Testosterone Naturally - Mitochondria, Insulin, and Fighting Back》* 第129集中，代謝專家 *Dr. Ben Bikman* 深入解析男性睪酮下降的生理機制，並提出自然改善的方法。

---

## 📌 主要內容整理

- *男性更年期（Andropause）*  
  - 與女性停經不同，男性睪酮下降是漸進式的。  
  - **Leydig 細胞**隨年齡效率降低，導致睪酮生成減少。  
  - **自由睪酮**下降速度更快，因為 **性激素結合球蛋白（SHBG）**隨年齡增加，綁住更多睪酮。

- *粒線體與睪酮生成*  
  - 粒線體是睪酮合成的能量核心。  
  - 功能受損（如氧化壓力、胰島素阻抗）會直接降低睪酮產量。  
  - 維持粒線體健康（運動、抗氧化營養素）有助於延緩睪酮下降。

- *胰島素的角色*  
  - 高胰島素與胰島素阻抗會抑制睪酮生成。  
  - 改善胰島素敏感度（低醣飲食、間歇性斷食）能支持睪酮水平。  
  - Dr. Bikman 強調 **代謝健康與性激素健康密不可分**。

- *生活方式干預*  
  - **阻力訓練**：刺激睪酮分泌並改善粒線體功能。  
  - **睡眠品質**：深層睡眠是睪酮生成的高峰期。  
  - **營養攝取**：蛋白質、健康脂肪（如Omega-3）、鋅、鎂等礦物質對睪酮合成至關重要。  
  - **壓力管理**：慢性壓力與高皮質醇會抑制睪酮。


## 🧩 整體觀點
Dr. Bikman 提出一個核心概念：*「睪酮下降不是單一問題，而是代謝健康全面失衡的表徵。」*  
透過改善粒線體功能、降低胰島素阻抗、優化生活方式，男性能在自然狀態下「對抗」睪酮下降，維持活力與健康。

  1. @AristoclesPlaton [1 likes]: The unqualified assertion that consciousness is solely function of brain metabolism is a conjecture. NDE reports are evidence that it is not. However, normal brain function is certainly dependant on respiration -> oxidative phosphorylation in mitochondria. And in so far as the content of our consciousness is normally a reflection of the information processing occurring in our brains, this appears to be so. 
A conjecture is an idea for which we have no idea of how to test it. The supposition that consciousness emerges solely from the activity in our brains is an example of a conjecture. 
An hypothesis is an idea for which we have good ideas about how to test it, but have not done so yet. 
A theory is an idea that has been tested, and it has not (yet) been possible to disprove the idea. Strong theories also come with convincing evidence in favor of the idea. A good theor always remains in principle falsifiable. 
A fact is a simple directly observable phenomenon, without theoretical structure, that is so elementary or anatomic that it cannot be denied. Compex ideas with an internal logical structure, often including the framework by which facts are to be interpreted, are not facts. Theory is as good as it gets in science. For example, the theory of evolution is not a fact. It is a theory, and a very good one. It has not been possible to falsify this theory despite heroic efforts of creationists and skeptical scientists trying their best for more than 150 years. There is a vast abundance of supporting evidence from every branch of relevant science. There is no good reason not to believe this theory. 
A scientist such as Martin. Picard really should not mix conjectures (for which there may even be counter evidence) with the theories about which he is an expert. This is misleading and shows an intellectual arrogance that he may one day come to regret.  

Martin Picard talks about certain medications that are prescribed in psychiatric medicine that damage mitochondrial function. He says, "There is (sic) specific classes of medication that impair mitochondrial energy transformation pretty significantly." I think he means to say "by a large amount" although this is not clear. Significance is a measure of probability, and tells us if the effect measured is likely or not to be an a statistical purturbation or rare misleading outcome. It says nothing about how large the effect is. The word "significant" should never be used to indicate a large effect.
